settings.excerpt:
Most of us do not lack time. We lack a stretch of it that nobody else has claimed. The day arrives already spoken for: a message before breakfast, a meeting that could have been a note, a small favour that takes the whole afternoon.

The quiet hour is not a productivity trick. It is a promise you make to the work that matters most to you, kept at the same time on most days, in the same place, with the door, the phone and the inbox closed.

You already have this hour. It is hiding in the edges of your week, in the half hour you lose to scrolling after lunch and the evening you spend tidying instead of starting. This chapter is about finding it, and the next eight are about keeping it.

Clara spent ten years as an editor at a busy newsroom, then left to write the books she kept wishing someone would hand her.

She writes in the mornings, from a small flat with a large window, and sends a short letter about reading and work every other Sunday.
